paras: The lynching of Jane Campbell was the burning of a Black woman at a stake by a mob near Dyke's Mill, Louisiana, in mid-September 1881. Campbell was accused of killing her two children, and after a coroner's jury blamed her for their deaths a mob of whites and blacks seized her and burned her alive. A Little Rock dispatch carried the story across the country, calling the crime and the punishment without parallel.

According to a Little Rock dispatch, Campbell lived near Dyke's Mill, not far from the line of Columbia County, Arkansas, and supported herself and two children by washing and cotton-picking. She was accused of becoming angry with the children, aged ten and twelve, over a trivial act of disobedience and beating them to death with a pine knot. Coroner Sykes held an inquest, and the jury found that the children died of wounds caused by a club in the hands of what the dispatch called 'an unnatural mother'.

After the verdict was announced and the cause of the deaths became generally known, a mob made up of blacks and whites gathered and seized Campbell. The widely reprinted dispatch said the mob dragged her from her cabin, tied her to a stake and, despite her screams and cries for mercy, roasted her alive. A separate dispatch dated at Dykes Mills on 17 September said instead that she was taken 'last night' from the officers who had her in charge and that fagots were piled about her. The same dispatch said the sheriff and a posse tried to arrest some of the mob but were fired on and driven off.
No report of arrests, an inquest into Campbell's death or any prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune printed the first report on 17 September, a special dispatch from Little Rock headed 'A Colored Woman Murders Two Children, and Is Roasted Alive by a Mob.' Over the next two weeks the same text ran in papers from New York and Savannah to Salt Lake City, often condensed into a single line of a news summary. The dispatch set the killing of the children beside the burning, closing with the line that 'the crime and punishment is without a parallel'.

Headlines differed in tone: the New-York Tribune called it 'Lawlessness in Louisiana', the Savannah Morning News 'Lynched by Roasting', and the Memphis Daily Appeal 'A Brutal Outrage', with the deck 'An Unnatural Mother Ruthlessly and Horrifically Dealt With'. The Ottawa Free Trader in Illinois headed its version 'A Louisiana Amusement', and the Connecticut Western News alone hedged that the burning was 'alleged'. Shorter items dropped the race of the mob, describing it as 'a mob of citizens' or 'a crowd of her neighbors'.

The two Louisiana papers in the coverage, the Donaldsonville Chief and the Morehouse Clarion, added no local detail and reprinted wire copy, the Clarion under the heading 'Almost Incredible'. The Washington People's Advocate also carried the Little Rock dispatch in its news column.

Accounts disagreed on where Campbell was seized: the Little Rock dispatch said from her cabin, the Dykes Mills dispatch from officers, and a Missouri brief from jail. The Little Rock version was second-hand, based on information received there, while the Dykes Mills dispatch was the only one to mention officers or a sheriff's posse. Some papers, including the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Litchfield Enquirer, placed the burning in Arkansas rather than Louisiana.

reader.title: Lynching of Jane Campbell
bases: A mob seized Jane Campbell, a Black woman accused of killing her two children, tied her to a stake and burned her to death (A3, A5, A14).

Every report says a mob burned her alive at a stake after a coroner's jury blamed her for the children's deaths (A5, A3); no lawful authority was involved, and one report says the mob drove off a sheriff's posse (A14).
The Little Rock dispatch (A3, A5) and a separate Dykes Mills dispatch (A14) agree that a mob burned her at a stake, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire dispatch
accounts.gist: After the inquest, when the cause of the children's deaths became known, a mob of whites and blacks dragged her from her cabin, tied her to a stake and roasted her alive.

accounts.label: Dykes Mills dispatch
accounts.gist: She was taken from the officers holding her 'last night', tied to a stake with fagots piled about her and slowly roasted; the sheriff's posse tried to make arrests and was fired on and driven off.

accounts.label: Brief news summaries
accounts.gist: Shortened items: a mob took her 'from jail' and burned her, or she was placed over a fire of pine knots.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Little Rock dispatch, which called her 'an unnatural mother' and said 'the crime and punishment is without parallel', setting the burning beside the killings.
The New-York Tribune headed the dispatch 'Lawlessness in Louisiana'.
Memphis headed it 'A Brutal Outrage' with the deck 'An Unnatural Mother Ruthlessly and Horrifically Dealt With'.
The Ottawa Free Trader headed it 'A Louisiana Amusement'; the Morehouse Clarion, 'Almost Incredible'.
Savannah headed it 'Lynched by Roasting'; others used 'Roasted Alive' or 'Unparalleled Crime and Punishment'.

versions.value: from the officers having her in charge

conflicts.note: The cabin version is one Little Rock dispatch reprinted widely and is second-hand ('information was received'); the officers version is a separate Dykes Mills dispatch; the jail version is a condensed brief.
The fuller dispatch places Dyke's Mill in Louisiana near the Columbia County, Arkansas line; the Arkansas versions appear to confuse the Little Rock dateline.
The versions do not contradict each other; the shorter briefs omit race.
